state.place: This website, read on a visit made for the reader's own work.

items.text: A large opening question with a photograph: what does a doorman actually do?
The story behind the idea, retold from Rory Sutherland's book Alchemy, with credit to him.
Six kinds of work a person does that a job description leaves out, each named with a one-line meaning.
Three questions to ask about any automation: what task is automated, what work remains, and who takes it on.
A table of real organisations that reduced roles because AI was to do the work, with what changed and what was reported afterwards.
A page per case: what sources reported, with quotes and links to archived copies, the site's own reading of what work may have been missed, a timeline, and the date it will be checked again.
An explanation of how cases are chosen, written and checked, including that AI agents do the work under fixed rules and what those rules are.
A printable one-page sheet of questions that helps a person write down the work they do beyond their job description.
A printable one-page sheet of questions for a manager to answer before automating a role, with a table of the kinds of work that may be lost.
A form to send in a report of a case, or to report an error in one.
A monthly email when cases are added or change.
A page about the person who runs the site.
A page on what personal data the site keeps and for how long.
A feed of new and changed cases for a feed reader.
A one-sentence definition of the doorman fallacy, with a line showing how to cite it.
For each kind of work a job description leaves out, an example from the hotel and an example from a present-day job affected by AI.
Signs that a decision is making this mistake, such as savings counted only on the visible task.
When replacing a task with AI or automation is the right call, with examples where the change worked.
All cases as a downloadable spreadsheet and data file, under a licence that allows reuse with credit.
A summary of all cases: how many are holding, under strain or reversed, by sector and by kind of missing work.
Ways to narrow the list of cases by outcome, sector, country and kind of missing work.
An overview of what is known so far about AI-linked job cuts and rehiring, with sources and cautions about survey figures.
A reading list: the book, related ideas such as Goodhart's law and tacit knowledge, and research.
Short articles that draw out patterns across several cases.
Practical next steps for someone whose role was cut: their rights, who to talk to, and how to describe their work to a new employer.
A step-by-step plan for automating a role while keeping its hidden work covered.
A slide deck and session plan, free to reuse, for running a workshop on the idea.
A page for journalists: contact, the definition, images and the terms for reuse.
Short answers to common questions, such as whether the site is against AI.
A page for each kind of missing work, listing the cases where it went missing.
Past monthly emails, readable on the site.
Short starting points for managers, for employees and for journalists.
A way to fill in the two question sheets on screen and save the answers.
A recipe for sourdough bread.
A login page for the site's staff.

state.place: This website's pages, each described by what a visitor does there.

items.text: A page for getting a first idea of what the site is and where to go next.
A page for understanding the idea well enough to explain it to someone else.
A page for looking over real cases where organisations reduced roles because of AI.
A page for reading one organisation's case in detail, with its sources.
A page for judging whether the cases can be trusted.
A page for preparing for a conversation about a role that may be automated.
A page for telling the site about a case it does not have.
A page for finding out who runs the site.
